summary: Describes the use of the Ed25519 and Ed448 digital signature algorithms in the Secure Shell protocol. It updates RFC 4253.

eli5.summary: SSH needs a way to prove who you are. This adds two modern signing methods, Ed25519 and Ed448, to the ways SSH can do that.

questions: how big is an ed25519 ssh public key
subtitle: Names and wire formats for using Ed25519 and Ed448 signatures as SSH public key algorithms.

tldr.problem: OpenSSH 6.5 and other implementations already used Ed25519 keys for server and user authentication, but the name and format were not formally specified. Ed448 had no SSH definition at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two public key algorithms, "ssh-ed25519" and "ssh-ed448". It gives their key and signature encodings as SSH strings and defers signing and verification to RFC 8032.
tldr.outcome: SSH gets two standardized signature-only algorithms, and standard SSH implementations SHOULD implement them. The RFC also adds an SSHFP code point for Ed448 keys.

today: RFC 8709 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It is not obsoleted and has no updates listed. It updates RFC 4253.

sections.title: Why Name Ed25519 and Ed448 in SSH
sections.content:
Secure Shell (SSH) is a secure remote-login protocol, and it lets implementations choose among an extensible variety of public key algorithms for identifying servers and users to one another. Ed25519 is a digital signature system. OpenSSH 6.5 introduced support for using it for server and user authentication, and other SSH implementations followed.

This RFC describes the method that OpenSSH and others implemented and formalizes the name ssh-ed25519. It also describes Ed448 and formalizes the name ssh-ed448. The RFC updates RFC 4253, the SSH transport layer specification.
sections.eli5: People were already using one kind of SSH signature, but nobody had written the rules down. This RFC writes them down and adds a second kind.

sections.title: The Two Public Key Algorithms
sections.content:
Both algorithms plug into SSH as public key algorithms in the sense of RFC 4253, Section 6.6. They are named ssh-ed25519 and ssh-ed448.

Each algorithm supports signing only, not encryption. The RFC says standard implementations of SSH SHOULD implement these signature algorithms, so support is encouraged but not strictly required.
sections.eli5: These keys can only sign things, like a stamp. They cannot be used to lock a secret message. Programs are encouraged to know how to use both.

sections.title: Key and Signature Encodings
sections.content:
A public key is encoded as two SSH strings: the algorithm name, then the key itself. For ssh-ed25519 the key is the 32-octet public key from RFC 8032, Section 5.1.5. For ssh-ed448 it is the 57-octet public key from Section 5.2.5.

A signature uses the same two-string layout: the algorithm name, then the signature. The ssh-ed25519 signature is 64 octets, produced as in RFC 8032 Section 5.1.6. The ssh-ed448 signature is 114 octets, produced as in Section 5.2.6.

The RFC does not define new signing math. Signatures are generated by the procedures in Sections 5.1.6 and 5.2.6 of RFC 8032, and verified by Sections 5.1.7 (Ed25519) and 5.2.7 (Ed448).
sections.eli5: Each key or signature is a little package with a label saying which kind it is, followed by the real bytes. The math for making and checking them is borrowed from another RFC.

sections.title: SSHFP DNS Records for Ed448
sections.content:
The SSHFP DNS resource record publishes SSH key fingerprints and is described in RFC 4255. Generating SSHFP records for ssh-ed25519 keys is already covered by RFC 7479, so this RFC covers Ed448.

An Ed448 public key is a 57-octet value representing a 455-bit y-coordinate of an elliptic curve point, plus a sign bit for the corresponding x-coordinate. The RFC shows an example record for an Ed448 key with a SHA-256 fingerprint: example.com. IN SSHFP 6 2 ( ... ). The 6 is the Ed448 algorithm code point and the 2 indicates SHA-256.
sections.eli5: A website can list the fingerprint of its key in a public phone book, so you can check you are talking to the right machine. This RFC says how to list the fingerprint for the new Ed448 kind of key.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added ssh-ed25519 and ssh-ed448 to the Public Key Algorithm Names in the "Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Parameters" registry, both referencing RFC 8709. This augments the names defined in RFC 4250, Section 4.11.3.

IANA also added value 6, described as Ed448, to the "SSHFP RR Types for public key algorithms" registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of SSH signature names got two new entries, and the list of fingerprint types got one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new security text of its own. The security considerations in RFC 4251, Section 9 apply to all SSH implementations, including those using Ed25519 and Ed448.

The considerations in RFC 8032, Section 8 and RFC 7479, Section 3 apply to all uses of Ed25519 and Ed448, including their use in SSH.
sections.eli5: The safety advice already written for SSH and for these signatures still applies. Nothing new is added.
